cues.text: A Soldier's Escort
Augustine Zhao Rong began his life as a soldier in the imperial Chinese army.
Assigned to escort the French missionary bishop Gabriel-Taurin Dufresse from Chengdu to Beijing for trial, Augustine was deeply moved by the bishop's calm dignity in persecution.
Over time, the encounter led him to seek baptism himself.
The First Chinese Diocesan Priest
Following his conversion, Augustine entered the seminary and was ordained, becoming the first native Chinese diocesan priest.

In 1815, renewed persecution swept through the region, and Augustine, like the bishop whose witness had first drawn him to the faith, was arrested, tortured, and died in prison for his own refusal to renounce Christianity.
Nearly Three Centuries of Martyrdom

Augustine's feast commemorates him together with 119 companions — 87 native Chinese Catholics and 33 Western missionaries — who died for the faith across a long span of Chinese history stretching from 1648 to 1930.
The company includes bishops, priests, and religious, but also ordinary catechists, farmers, a cook, a widow, a seventy-nine-year-old man, and a child of only nine.
Waves of Persecution
The Church in China endured repeated, often prolonged, periods of legal suppression across these centuries, forcing communities to worship in secret for extended stretches.

The single deadliest episode came during the Boxer Rebellion of 1900, when anti-foreign, anti-Christian uprisings killed tens of thousands of Chinese Christians and missionaries alike, a catastrophe reflected in the presence of numerous Boxer-era martyrs among this same canonized group.
Suspicion of Foreign Loyalty
Both Chinese-born and foreign-born martyrs in this group were frequently targeted less for their private religious belief than for the perception, however unfair.
Christianity represented an extension of Western political and colonial influence into China—a persistent and painful tension between authentic Chinese Catholic identity and outside suspicion.
This tension shaped the Church's difficult history in the country for centuries.
Legacy

Pope John Paul II canonized all 120 martyrs together on 1 October 2000, presenting them as a single witness to the endurance of the Chinese Catholic Church across nearly three hundred years of intermittent, often brutal persecution.
Augustine Zhao Rong, the sole individually named saint in the group's title, stands as a particular symbol of the Chinese Church's own native clergy.
He was a former soldier whose conversion, sparked by a foreign missionary's courage, in turn cost him his own life for the same faith.
